initial_presentation: The patient was a one-year-old male. His parents and elder sister, who were not related by blood, were also part of the study. The patient underwent various physical examinations and tests, including blood gas analysis, blood ammonia testing, plasma acylcarnitine profiling, urinary organic acid analysis, and brainstem auditory evoked potential (BAEP) studies. His family members only had physical examinations. The acylcarnitine profile was analyzed using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry, and urinary organic acids were analyzed using gas chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Blood gas analysis was performed with an automated analyzer, and BAEP was recorded using an electromyogram device. Written informed consent for data collection and publication was obtained from the parents, and the study was approved by the Ethical Committee of Quanzhou Children’s Hospital of Fujian, adhering to HIPAA regulations. The patient, a Chinese Han boy, initially presented to the dermatology department at the age of one year with a skin rash around the periorbital and perioral areas and was treated for eczema. Three weeks later, he was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with severe tachypnea, moaning, and heart failure. The rash had spread to his limbs, neck, and groin. Capillary blood gas analysis revealed metabolic acidosis with a pH of 6.98, a base excess of -26 mmol/L, bicarbonate level of 3.9 mmol/L, an anion gap of 25.2 mmol/L, elevated lactate of 13.1 mmol/L (normal < 2 mmol/L), and elevated ammonia of 152.0 μmol/L (normal < 47 μmol/L). Biochemical tests on admission showed low ornithine (15.99 μmol/L; normal 42–325 μmol/L) and a plasma acylcarnitine profile with low free carnitine and significant increases in C5-OH, C5-OH/C0, C5-OH/C8, C3/C2, and C3/C0. The urinary organic acid profile showed excessive excretion of 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid, acetylglycine, propionylglycine, 3-methylcrotonylglycine, methylcrotonylglycine, 3-hydroxybutyric acid, pyruvic acid, and lactic acid. Increased levels of 2-keto-3-methyl-pentanoic acid and 2-keto-isocaproic acid suggested a metabolic disorder of branched-chain amino acids. The patient was treated with biotin (20 mg bid), which led to the resolution of the skin rash and normalization of acid–base balance within five days. Subsequently, the level of C5-OH decreased, and the urinary organic acid profile showed undetectable levels of acetylglycine, propionylglycine, 3-methylcrotonylglycine, and methylcrotonylglycine. During the acute episode, a BAEP study indicated significantly prolonged wave I latency and I–V interpeak latency intervals, with increased bilateral thresholds: left at 50 dB nHL and right at 60 dB nHL, indicating bilateral hearing impairment. A cattle encephalon glycoside and ignotin injection was administered. After 43 days of biotin therapy, a repeat BAEP study showed that the bilateral thresholds had decreased to 30 dB nHL, indicating improvement in hearing.

A 64-year-old Chinese male presented with multiple dark-brown papules on the scalp for 1 year. The lesions were asymptomatic and gradually increased in number over time. He had a history of androgenetic alopecia (AGA) for a decade and used topical 5% minoxidil for only 1 month, 5 years ago. The patient was otherwise healthy with no relevant family history. Physical examination showed discrete, 1- to 3-mm, flat-topped, brownish papules over the crown and vertex area of the scalp. Dermoscopic examination revealed a whitish scar-like center surrounded by brownish dots or brown fine streaks radiating from the center, located in a background of hair and scalp alteration typical of AGA.

A 12-year-old male presented with a 6-day history of pain and redness in the left eye. Initial examination showed a best-corrected visual acuity of 1.0 in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination identified 2+ flare and occasional cells in the anterior chamber, while the funduscopic examination showed no inflammatory signs in the posterior segment of the left eye. The right eye showed no abnormalities. Ten days later, inflammatory findings were noted in the right eye. Both eyes exhibited conjunctival and ciliary injections, 1+ flare, 3+ cells in the anterior chamber, and mutton fat keratic precipitates. Additionally, redness and swelling of the optic disc were observed in both eyes.

In early October 2012, a 66-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of an itchy rash initially on his lower limbs, which gradually spread to cover most of his body. There was no involvement of mucosal areas or other systemic symptoms. His medical history included hypertension managed with irbesartan. Physical examination revealed scaly, annular, erythematous-violaceous maculopapules on the palms and soles. Lesions in pressure areas exhibited a palpable purpuric macular appearance.

A three-month-old female child was brought to our hospital due to concerns about apparent blindness. The child had a history of frequent episodes of flexor spasms accompanied by eye twitching since one and a half months of age. These episodes occurred approximately five to six times daily and were associated with drooling. According to the parents, the child did not respond to light or sound. She was the second child in a family with no consanguinity, born at full term through a normal delivery. There was no history of jaundice, fever, or convulsions in the immediate neonatal period. Upon examination, the child exhibited global developmental delay. Her head circumference was in the 10th percentile. Ophthalmic examination showed that the child did not respond to or follow bright light, and both pupils had very sluggish reactions. The anterior segments and vitreous of both eyes were normal. Fundus examination revealed bilateral optic nerve colobomas with variable-sized discrete dome-shaped pale areas with sharp borders (chorioretinal lacunae) located just nasal to the optic discs. The fovea was unaffected in both eyes.

A three-year-old male presented with increased seizure frequency despite being on multiple anti-seizure medications. The patient was admitted for further evaluation. His past medical history includes epilepsy, infantile spasms, developmental delay, gastroesophageal reflux, laryngomalacia, and dysphagia. The mother reported no prenatal or neonatal complications. The child experienced infantile spasms at 11 months of age and was treated with prednisone. Clobazam was initiated for seizure prevention, but myoclonic seizures developed after two months. Adjusting the clobazam dose reduced seizure frequency. At 16 months, tonic-clonic seizures began, and a ketogenic diet was introduced, reducing seizures from 20 to 10 episodes per day. Cannabinol was added at age two, further decreasing seizures to fewer than five per day. However, seizure frequency later increased to over 10 per day. At two years and three months, levetiracetam was started without significant improvement. Three months later, zonisamide was introduced, also without significant effects. The ketogenic diet was discontinued, and the zonisamide dose was increased, reducing seizure frequency to four to five episodes per day.

A 63-year-old man presented with a two-month history of widespread redness and thickening of the skin, sparing the axillary and inguinal regions. Neurological examination revealed muscle wasting in the interosseous muscles of the hands, ulnar claw deformity, tingling sensations in the hands and feet, and thickening of the ulnar and fibular nerves. There was significant swelling in the hands and feet. The patient reported no prior skin conditions or recent exposure to new medications or allergens.

A 41-year-old Muslim man from South Africa presented with widespread patchy skin discoloration. He was born to parents who are second-degree relatives. He reported the onset of gradually increasing widespread darkening of the skin starting from his trunk, followed by patchy lightening and loss of skin color from the age of 6 years, affecting his entire body. Recently, he observed a few light-colored spots on his forehead and balding scalp. Skin examination showed widespread net-like dark pigmentation covering the entire body, sparing the palms, soles, backs of hands, feet, face, and a small area on the chest which retained his original skin color. The light-colored spots were well-defined, varied in size from 4 mm to about 2 cm in diameter. Scattered dark, rough papules were noted on the extremities and proximal inner arms near the armpits, which had been present for the past 4 years. All skin changes were asymptomatic with no blistering, ulceration, thinning, mixed skin changes, scaling, or oozing. Palms, soles, mucous membranes, hair, and nails appeared normal. The patient reported no sensitivity to sunlight, systemic issues, inflammatory skin conditions, or growth delays.

A 9-year-old Chinese girl presented with pain in the posterior part of the left mandibular region and a nodule with pus discharge, noted one month prior to her visit. The patient exhibited normal growth without any height or developmental abnormalities. Physical examination identified a nodule with pus discharge and swelling under the left side of the chin. Applying gentle pressure to the surrounding tissue resulted in thick purulent drainage from the central punctum. Intraoral examination showed red and swollen alveolar mucosa in the region of the primary left mandibular second molar (#75), which was only partially erupted. All teeth in the mixed dentition displayed abnormal shapes, except for the bilateral permanent incisors in both the maxillary and mandibular regions, which were misaligned. The crowns of the primary canines and the primary maxillary first molars (#54 and 64) were enlarged, bulbous, and malformed with 2 or 3 cusps, resembling either fusion or germination. Tooth #64 exhibited level III mobility without any positive signs on percussion or palpation. The primary maxillary second molars (#55 and 65) and the primary right mandibular first molar (#84) were similarly enlarged with developmental grooves dividing the crowns into various lobules. Additionally, small tooth-like structures were observed around tooth #84. The first permanent molars lacked clearly defined cusps, resembling the tied end of a sausage. Teeth #75 and 85 were only partially erupted. According to her guardians, the patient's incisors began to erupt at age 4 and had never been replaced, indicating congenital absence of the primary incisors. Her parents also noted that the eruption of her primary dentition was delayed compared to normal children.

A 47-year-old female arrived at the emergency department experiencing multiple episodes of sudden dizziness and near-fainting. The initial episode happened one week before her visit while she was driving; she managed to stop the car safely, and the dizziness subsided after one minute. She continued to have episodes of near-fainting, which increased in severity and duration, prompting her visit to the emergency department. She reported no palpitations, shortness of breath, chest pain, or complete loss of consciousness. Physical examination showed no abnormalities. Her medical history was clear, and she was not taking any medications. She was an active smoker with a 10-pack-year history and consumed minimal alcohol. A detailed family history did not indicate any instances of sudden cardiac death or heart disease.
